props.title: Our Sunhi

sections.content: **Our Sunhi (2013)** (2013) represents Hong Sang-soo at his most playfully recursive. Like his masterful The Day He Arrives (2011), Hong uses repetition and overlapping conversations to expose how differently men perceive and project onto women. Three men - a professor, an ex-boyfriend, and a younger admirer - each claim to "truly understand" Sunhi, yet their contradictory descriptions reveal more about themselves than her. Hong's trademark long takes and soju-soaked conversations create an intimate atmosphere that makes the comedy both biting and sympathetic.

sections.content: Hong's exploration of male gaze and projection finds kinship in other contemporary Asian cinema, particularly in **Happy Hour** (2015) by Ryusuke Hamaguchi and **Burning** (2018) by Lee Chang-dong. These films share a careful observation of how men construct narratives around women, though Hong's approach is distinctly more comedic. His characteristic zoom shots and repeated scenes serve to highlight the absurdity of each man's certainty about understanding Sunhi.

The film's structural playfulness recalls Hong's other works like In Another Country (2012) and **On the Beach at Night Alone** (2017), where narrative repetition becomes a tool for examining perspective and truth. The recurring restaurant scene in **Our Sunhi**, where each man separately meets with Sunhi in the same location, becomes increasingly revealing and darkly humorous with each iteration. sections.content: **Our Sunhi** marks a refinement of techniques Hong had been developing since **Virgin Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors** (2000). His signature style - long takes, minimal camera movement punctuated by sudden zooms, and naturalistic dialogue - reaches a new level of precision here. The film's deceptively simple approach masks a complex exploration of memory, perception, and self-deception that would influence later works like **The Woman Who Ran** (2020) and **Introduction** (2021).
